body.p: REMARKS

This Amendment is in response to the Office Action dated June 20, 2024. Applicant has amended claims 1, 11, 21, and 22. Claims 1 - 5, 8 - 15, and 18 - 22 remain pending upon entry of this Amendment. Applicant respectfully requests reconsideration in view of the amendments and the following remarks.

In an Applicant-initiated Examiner Interview on September 17, 2024, Examiner Etsub D. Berhanu and Applicant's representative, Ryan W. Kobs (Reg. No. 68,237), discussed therejection of claims 1-5, 8-15, and 18-22 under 35 U.S.C. § 112(a) and the rejection of claims 1-5, 8-15, and 18-22 under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as allegedly being unpatentable over U.S. Patent Application Publication No. 2009/0082691 by Denison et al. (hereinafter, "Denison") in view of U.S. Patent Application Publication No. 2007/0197930 by Sarkela (hereinafter, "Sarkela"), as evidenced by U.S. Patent No. 5,601,090 by Musha (hereinafter, "Musha"), further in view of U.S. Patent Application Publication No. 2008/0228100 by Navakatikyan (hereinafter, "Navakatikyan"). Specifically, claim 1 and alternative language was discussed with respect to the requirements under 35 U.S.C. § 112(a) and the cited references.

Examiner Berhanu and Applicant's representative reached agreement that claims 1-5, 8- 15, and 18-22 satisfy the requirements under 35 U.S.C. § 112(a). No formal agreement was reached with respect to the rejections under 35 U.S.C. § 103, but Examiner Berhanu appears to agree that the cited references, alone or in any proper combination, do not disclose the subject matter of amended independent claims 1, 11, 21, and 22. No exhibits were presented and no demonstrations were conducted during the interview. Applicant thanks Examiner Berhanu for taking the time to discuss the application with Applicant's representative.
Claim Interpretation Under 35 U.S.C. 4 112

In the Office Action, the Examiner noted that 35 U.S.C. § 112 (f) has been invoked when interpreting claim 21. Applicant does not necessarily acquiesce to the identified structures, materials, or acts for each claim limitation, but Applicant acknowledges the Examiner's interpretation under 35 U.S.C. § 112 (f).
In the Office Action, the Examiner rejected claims 1-5, and 8-15, and 18-22 under 35

U.S.C. § 112(a), asserting that claims 1-5, and 8-15, and 18-22 are not supported by Applicant's specification. The Examiner asserted that "there is no description of how a selected second frequency band would be incorporated into the method of determining a control signal for the therapy device."I

As discussed above in the Interview Summary, the Examiner agreed that the claims satisfy the requirements under 35 U.S.C. § 112(a). For example, paragraph [0007] of Applicant's specification discloses that "[d]ifferent frequency bands of a bioelectrical brain signal may be associated with different brain activity of the patient" and that "[t]he brain activity may be, for example, associated with a patient-initiated state (e.g., e.g., a movement state, a speech state, or a sleep state), a patient condition (e.g., a disease state), or the occurrence of a specific symptom of a patient condition." Paragraph [0044] discloses that "spectral characteristics may be, for example, stored by a device as biomarkers indicative of a particular patient state, such as normal or pathological behaviors, responses to medications or other therapies, including electrical therapies, or both." Also, paragraph [0008] states that "[t]he processor may control therapy delivery to the patient based on the determined patient state, monitor a patient condition based on the determined patient state, generate a patient diagnosis (e.g., determines a patient condition sub-type) based on the determined patient state, or any combination thereof." Since generally therapy delivery can be controlled based on any combination of states or conditions that may be associated with different frequency bands, Applicant's specification provides written description support for at least these reasons.

Accordingly, for at least the reasons discussed above, claims 1-5, and 8-15, and 18-22 are supported by Applicant's specification, in accordance with 35 U.S.C. § 112(a). Applicant respectfully requests reconsideration and withdrawal of all rejections under 35 U.S.C. § 112(a).
In addition, for at least these reasons, Applicant's current patent application is an

application which is also disclosed in the prior application (the parent or original nonprovisional application or provisional application). The disclosure of the invention in the parent application and in the current application comply with the requirements of 35 U.S.C. § 112. Accordingly, Applicant's originally claim for priority is correct.

The Office Action rejected claims 1-5, 8-15, and 18-22 under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as
allegedly being unpatentable over by Denison in view of Sarkela, as evidenced by Musha, and further in view of Navakatikyan.

Without conceding the merits of the rejection, Applicant has amended the claims solely to advance prosecution towards allowance. Applicant respectfully traverses the rejections to the extent the rejections are applicable to the amended claims. The applied references, alone or in any combination, do not disclose or suggest the subject matter defined by Applicant's claims, and there would have been no apparent reason that would have caused one of ordinary skill in the art to modify the applied references to arrive at the claimed subject matter.

The Examiner cited Navakatikyan to correct an admitted deficiency of Denison in view of Sarkela to disclose or suggest "one or more of a peak width less than or equal to a first threshold value or a peak width greater than or equal to a second threshold value" as recited by Applicant's claim 1, for example. The Examiner further asserted that "the method does not require the one or more processors to determine that a biomarker indicative of a first patient state is present in the bioelectrical brain signal, nor does it require the one or more processors to determine a width of a peak."2

Applicant notes that amended independent claim 1 recites, inter alia, "wherein determining the first characteristic comprises determining, as the first predetermined characteristic within the first distribution, a first peak width less than or equal to a first threshold value or greater than or equal to a second threshold value" and "wherein determining the second characteristic comprises determining, as the second predetermined characteristic within the second distribution, a second peak width less than or equal to a third threshold value or greater than or equal to a fourth threshold value." Therefore, amended claim 1 does require determining "a first peak width" and "a second peak width," as requested by the Office.
Indeed, neither Navakatikyan, nor any proper combination of the cited references,

discloses "determining, as [a] first predetermined characteristic within [a] first distribution, a first peak width less than or equal to a first threshold value or greater than or equal to a second threshold value" and "determining, as [a] second predetermined characteristic within [a] second
2 Office Action dated June 20, 2024, page 10.

distribution, a second peak width less than or equal to a third threshold value or greater than or equal to a fourth threshold value." The Examiner characterized Navakatikyan as "identifying a biomarker comprising a unimodal peak or a bimodal peak."3 Contrary to the Examiner's characterization, Navakatikyan instead describes calculations to determine, "the amplitude of a peak and a trough in each data group,"4 which includes determining "the time interval between the peak and/or the trough."5 Navakatikyan does not describe determining any peak width. Since Navakatikyan does not disclose this feature, one of ordinary skill in the art would have had no rational reason to modify Denison, Sarkela, Musha, or any combination thereof to arrive at the subject matter of amended independent claim 1.

For at least these reasons, the cited references alone or in any reasonable combination, do not disclose or suggest the subject matter defined by amended claim 1, and there would have been no apparent reason that would have caused one of ordinary skill in the art to modify the applied references to arrive at the claimed subject matter. Amended independent claims 11, 21, and 22 include subject similar to that recited by claim 1 and arguments with regard to claim 1 apply equally to independent claims 11, 21, and 22.

For at least the reasons discussed above, amended independent claims 1, 11, 21, and 22 are patentable over the cited references. The dependent claims incorporate the requirements of the respective independent claims.6 Accordingly, the dependent claims are likewise patentable.
For at least these reasons, Applicant's amended claims 1 - 5, 8 - 15, and 18 - 22 are
patentable under 35 U.S.C. § 103. Applicant therefore respectfully requests reconsideration and withdrawal of all rejections under 35 U.S.C. § 103.
All claims in this application are in condition for allowance. Applicant respectfully requests reconsideration and prompt allowance of all pending claims.

Applicant does not concede that the subject matter encompassed by the claims prior to this Response is unpatentable over the art cited by the Office Action. While several distinctions have been noted over the art of record, Applicant notes that there may be several other
